title: Resources
Bootstrapping with Pokemon Cards
text:
Description
Grab your students’ attentions with a deck of Pokemon cards and start bootstrapping! Using physical, recognizable cards will allow students to identify what it means to sample with replacement. Plus, cards are easily shuffled and scrambled.
There are numeric values (HP - found in the top right corner) and categorical values (type, rarity, colour) that you can record data for on each card.

title: Bootstrapping with Pokemon Cards
text:
Learning outcomes:
After the activity, students will be able to:

Identify that bootstrapping involves sampling with replacement
Calculate bootstrap sample means/proportions

title: Bootstrapping with Pokemon Cards
text:
Materials Needed

Document Camera
50(ish) Pokemon (or other) cards.
Pen/paper or a white board

(Psst.. Are you at UBC? Ask Grace for a deck!)

title: Bootstrapping with Pokemon Cards
text:
Directions
Before class

Calculate a population quantity (mean or proportion) of all cards in your deck. Record this somewhere so you can reference it in class.

In class

After introducing the bootstrapping algorithm in lecture, create a research question related to the Pokemon card (population) deck. For example, what is the mean HP of my deck? Or, what proportion of my cards are electric type?
Take a small sample (10ish) from your deck (I ask 10 students to each pick one card). Put the rest aside and tell students that you won’t touch any more cards for bootstrapping. Show the 10 cards under the document cam, emphasizing that each one is a unique Pokemon. Note the measurement of interest (HP, type)
Calculate the sample mean/proportion of the 10 cards. Record it.
Take the 10 cards and shuffle them. Draw one card, record the value of interest, and put the card back into the deck.
Shuffle, choose, and record 9 more times. Note when the same card is chosen more than once!
Take the 10 measurements and calculate the bootstrap mean/proportion. Record this on the paper/board as the first bootstrap mean/proportion.
Repeat steps 5-7 once more, emphasizing that you did NOT take a new sample. Record this on the paper/board as the first bootstrap mean/proportion.
Compare and contrast the two bootstrap estimates to each other.
They will likely differ.
Compare the two bootstrap means/proportions to the sample mean/proportion.
With more samples, the bootstrap sample means/proportions would average out to this value.
Compare the two bootstrap means/proportions to the population mean/proportion you calculated before class.
These may be quite different as the bootstrap means/proportions center around the sample mean, not the population one. If you get unlucky with your initial sample, then the bootstrap samples will be different from the population too.

Statistics and data science classes don’t have to be boring!
On this website, you will find ideas for activities and resources to help you inject life back into your classroom.

title: Bootstrapping with Carrots: Shiny Applet + Activity
text:
Description
Connect the dots between the population, sample, and bootstrap sample with this interactive applet.
A farmer has been tending to a large field of carrots and would like to evaluate their growth. The farmer is only willing to give you 30 random carrots to assess their growth.
This applet and associated activity was tested with small group of undergraduate students.

title: Bootstrapping with Carrots: Shiny Applet + Activity
text:
Learning outcomes:
After the activity, students will be able to:

Identify that bootstrapping involves sampling with replacement
Calculate bootstrap sample means/proportions
Compare and contrast the population, sampling, and bootstrap distributions
Construct and interpret 95% plausible ranges

title: Sampling the Globe
text:
Description
How can you determine the proportion of the Earth that is covered in water using only a globe?
You may be tempted to start calculating complex areas, but the answer is much easier - we can use simple random sampling!
In this activity, students will throw around an inflatable globe to obtain random samples. There is also a simple, optional applet that can help you keep track and visualize the samples as you go.

title: Sampling the Globe
text:
Learning outcomes:
After the activity, students will be able to:

Define and recall the weak law of large numbers
Identify a real application of the weak law of large numbers

title: Sampling the Globe
text:
Materials Needed

Inflatable globe
Link to globe water tracker OR pen/paper/white board

(Psst.. Are you at UBC? Ask Grace for the inflatable globe!)

title: Sampling the Globe
text:
Directions

Set the scene:


Suppose you wash up on deserted island with no internet connection. A pirate appears and offers you the opportunity to catch a ride back with them to the nearest city so long as you can answer one question: what proportion of the Earth’s surface is water? Unfortunately, you’ve bumped your head and cannot remember basic trivia. The pirate offers you a globe to assist in your answer. How can you get off of this island?


Students will throw the ball around and indicate whether or not the point under their index finger is LAND or WATER. You can keep track of the LAND vs WATER count, stopping every so often to get the sample mean. You can also track it on this app here: globe water tracker

After about 10 or so points, you will see it start to converge to the true value or 71%.
